results.summary: This design generates a VGA video signal that animates columns of pink hearts transitioning on and off the screen. It is implemented in Verilog using the VGA Playground environment and is intended to be tested by running the simulation and observing the output. The design requires a VGA display connected to the Tiny VGA PMOD pinout. It is a simple, cute animation project with no additional features or complexity.

This is an analog self-biased single-ended folded cascode operational transconductance amplifier (OTA) designed for high gain and high bandwidth. It uses a beta-multiplier to provide a rough current source and a folded cascode OTA architecture. The design has differential inputs VIN and VIP and a single-ended output VOUT, and it is tested by applying a differential signal and observing the output with an oscilloscope. It is a purely analog design with no digital components.

This design displays a Christmas tree on a VGA monitor. It is implemented in Verilog and uses the Tiny VGA pinout. The documentation is extremely minimal, consisting only of the title and repeated phrases, so it is unclear how the design works or how to test it beyond connecting a VGA display. It appears to be a simple festive animation.

This analog tile integrates two independent circuits: a current-controlled ring oscillator VCO and a differential amplifier, sharing a single bias/control pin. Both circuits are permanently powered from 1.8V and are tested via separate analog and digital pins. External testing requires an Analog Discovery 3 or equivalent equipment (DC supply, function generator, oscilloscope) and a breakout board to access the chip's pins. The design is notable for combining two analog functions in a single tile under pin constraints.

This design generates a VGA video signal displaying a checkered pattern that bounces back and forth on the screen. It is based on a modified checkers example and is implemented in Verilog using the VGA Playground. Testing is done by compiling in VGA Playground and observing the output on a VGA display. The design requires a VGA monitor connected to the Tiny VGA PMOD pinout.

This project implements a 16-bit Galois linear feedback shift register (LFSR) with configurable width (4, 8, 12, or 16 bits), selectable primitive polynomials, and nibble-serial seed loading. It provides a full 16-bit output, with the LSB available as a serial bit. The design requires no external hardware but can drive an LED or logic analyzer for PRBS verification. It is a flexible pseudorandom number generator suitable for testing and cryptographic applications.

This design implements an 8-bit signed Baugh-Wooley multiplier, originally developed as part of a neural network project. It accepts two 8-bit operands through ui_in and uio_in, and outputs the 16-bit product split across uo_out (lower 8 bits) and uio_out (upper 8 bits). The multiplier uses a tree reduction structure and supports two's complement signed multiplication. It requires no external hardware and can be tested by applying operands and reading the result after one clock cycle.

This project implements a programmable I/O (PIO) block inspired by the RP2350's PIO but not compatible with it. It provides 8 GPIO inputs and 8 GPIO outputs, along with control signals for loading and addressing. The documentation is very sparse, stating only that it is modelled after the RP2350 PIO and that testing is tricky, with more explanation to come. It is a complex digital design that likely requires external hardware and software support to use effectively.

This design generates stochastic melodies using two Markov chains, one for note selection and one for note duration, on a pentatonic scale. It uses a 16-bit LFSR as an entropy source and includes adjustable BPM and selectable probability matrices. The output is a PWM signal that can drive a buzzer, and the design requires a PMOD buzzer for audio output. It is a creative application of Markov chains and LFSR for algorithmic music generation.

This project implements an ECG front-end for measuring electrocardiogram signals, using a folded cascode architecture. It includes differential inputs (INp and INm), a reference (ref), a Vref pin, an output (OUT), and a driven right leg output (OUTDRL). Testing involves connecting ECG electrodes to the inputs and observing the output on an oscilloscope, with proper biasing of the reference pins. The design is a specialized analog front-end for biomedical signal acquisition.
